title: Council of Nicaea Establishes Orthodoxy/Heresy Framework
description: The Council of Nicaea (325 CE), convened by Constantine I, established the Nicene Creed as the doctrinal standard for Christianity and formally defined the Arian position as heresy. The Council's procedures — assembling bishops to rule on doctrine, reaching a consensus definition, and condemning dissent — established the institutional framework for identifying and combating heresy that would later underlie both medieval inquisitions and the prosecution of witchcraft as a form of heresy. The Council also addressed questions of church discipline, creating a model of hierarchical ecclesiastical authority that could be deployed to root out doctrinal error. Its long-term significance for witch prosecution lies in establishing the very concept of bounded orthodoxy versus heretical deviation.
historiographical_note: Norman Cohn's Europe's Inner Demons traces the long arc from Nicaea's establishment of heresy categories through to the witch-hunt, arguing that the institutional machinery of heresy prosecution was a precondition for organized witch-hunting.
source_method: Published scholarship; Council of Nicaea canons; Norman Cohn, Europe's Inner Demons (1975)
